questions.title: `Semaphore(3)` was used to allow only 3 threads to run at once
questions.question: In the lecture, a Semaphore(3) was used to allow only 3 threads to run at once (like a parking lot with 3 spots). If instead you initialize Semaphore(0), what happens when a thread immediately calls acquire() on it?

options.optionText: It behaves exactly like Semaphore(1)
It raises an error because 0 is not allowed
It passes through instantly since there's nothing to block
It blocks immediately, since there are zero permits available — the thread waits until something else calls release()

questions.title: For problems like "print first, then second, then third in strict order using multiple threads," why can a semaphore be used to enforce ordering, not just capacity limits?
questions.question: For problems like "print first, then second, then third in strict order using multiple threads," why can a semaphore be used to enforce ordering, not just capacity limits?

options.optionText: Semaphores cannot be used for ordering — only Lock can do this
Because semaphores are faster than locks
Because acquire() in one thread can be made to wait for a release() called by a different thread, effectively passing a signal/permission from one thread to another
Because semaphores automatically sort threads by their function name

questions.title: What is the guaranteed printed order?
questions.question:
What is the guaranteed printed order?
```python
import threading

sem = threading.Semaphore(0)

def waiter():
    sem.acquire()
    print("B")

t = threading.Thread(target=waiter)
t.start()
print("A")
sem.release()
t.join()
```

options.optionText: It will hang forever and print nothing
B then A, always
Random — could be A then B, or B then A
A then B, always

questions.title: This is meant to make "second" print only after "first," using semaphores, but it has a bug.
questions.question:
This is meant to make "second" print only after "first," using semaphores, but it has a bug:

```python
import threading

class Foo:
    def __init__(self):
        self.sem = threading.Semaphore(1)  # BUG is here

    def first(self):
        print("first")
        self.sem.release()

    def second(self):
        self.sem.acquire()
        print("second")
```

What is wrong and what's the fix?

options.optionText: threading.Semaphore should be threading.Lock
The methods first and second should be swapped
Semaphore(1) should be Semaphore(0) — since second() must be forced to wait until first() releases it. Starting at 1 lets second() run immediately without waiting
second() should call release() instead of acquire()

questions.title: For the "ZeroEvenOdd" problem (three threads: one prints only 0s, one prints only evens, one prints only odds, in strict interleaved order), which setup is closest to correct?
questions.question: For the "ZeroEvenOdd" problem (three threads: one prints only 0s, one prints only evens, one prints only odds, in strict interleaved order), which setup is closest to correct?

options.optionText: It cannot be done with semaphores; only Condition will work
Use time.sleep() with carefully tuned delays to control the order
Use one single Lock shared by all three threads with no other coordination
Use three separate semaphores — e.g., a zero_sem starting at 1, and even_sem/odd_sem starting at 0 — so each thread's release() signals exactly which thread should run next

questions.title: What is a "critical section" in the context of threading.Lock?
questions.question: What is a "critical section" in the context of threading.Lock?

options.optionText: A section of code that never has bugs
The block of code that only one thread can execute at a time while holding the lock
Any function that uses threads
The part of code that runs fastest

questions.title: `threading.Lock` cause a deadlock
questions.question: Why does a plain threading.Lock cause a deadlock if the same thread tries to acquire it twice (e.g., a locked function calling another locked function)?

options.optionText: The second acquire() call raises an exception immediately
Python doesn't allow nested function calls
A Lock has no memory of who is holding it, so it just waits forever for a release that never comes from itself
Locks can only be used once per program

questions.title: Python Concurrency 3 - What will this print?
questions.question:
What will this print?

```python
import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def increment():
    global counter
    for _ in range(50_000):
        with lock:
            counter += 1

t1 = threading.Thread(target=increment)
t2 = threading.Thread(target=increment)
t1.start(); t2.start()
t1.join(); t2.join()

print(counter)
```

options.optionText: It will raise a deadlock error
A random number less than 100,000 each time it runs
100000, every single time

questions.title: The following code is supposed to safely reserve seats but has a bug. What is wrong?
questions.question:
The following code is supposed to safely reserve seats but has a bug. What is wrong?
```python
import threading

class BookingSystem:
    def __init__(self, seats):
        self.available_seats = seats
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def reserve(self, num_seats):
        if self.available_seats >= num_seats:
            with self.lock:
                pass
            self.available_seats -= num_seats
            return True
        return False
```

options.optionText: There is no bug, this code is correct
reserve should be a @staticmethod
threading.Lock() should be threading.RLock()

The check (if self.available_seats >= num_seats) and the update (self.available_seats -= num_seats) are NOT both inside the with self.lock: block, so two threads can still race between the check and the update

questions.question: A function outer() acquires a lock and then calls inner(), which also tries to acquire the same lock, from the same thread. Which tool correctly avoids deadlock here?
